title: Canada | PCMLTFA Compliance Program and FINTRAC Reporting
tagline: Run a Canadian bank's PCMLTFA program: KYC, PEPs, STRs, cash and EFT reports, directives, sanctions and FINTRAC's 2026 penalty regime.
sectors: Banks and federally regulated deposit-taking institutions
Payments, wire transfer and correspondent operations
Bank compliance, financial intelligence and audit
description:
This quest teaches staff at Canadian banks how the **Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (PCMLTFA)** and its **Regulations** work in practice, as supervised and enforced by **FINTRAC**, Canada's financial intelligence unit. It also covers the **Ministerial directives** issued by the Minister of Finance, the reporting links to Canada's **sanctions laws**, information sharing under **section 11.01**, and the changes made on **26 March 2026** by the Strengthening Canada's Immigration System and Borders Act: effective, risk-based programs, much higher penalties, and mandatory compliance agreements and public compliance orders.

The Regulations require every bank to keep a **written, ongoing compliance training program** for its employees and agents, with a documented plan for delivering it (paragraphs 156(1)(d) and (e)). This quest is built for that audience: front-line and branch staff, onboarding teams, payments operations, financial intelligence analysts, compliance officers, auditors and senior managers.

Across five stages you follow a fictional team at Maplecrest Bank in Toronto, Richmond and Montréal, and study real FINTRAC penalty notices against Canadian banks.

This quest builds knowledge of the law and FINTRAC's expectations; it does not replace your institution's own AML/ATF policies, procedures or advice from your compliance team.
audience: Branch, teller and contact centre staff at Canadian banks who deal with clients or handle cash
Account opening and onboarding teams handling individuals, corporations, trusts and PEPs
Payments, wire transfer and correspondent operations staff who file EFT reports and apply directives
Financial intelligence analysts and investigators who decide on suspicious transaction reports
Compliance officers, internal auditors and senior managers who own or test the PCMLTFA program
outcomes: Explain the PCMLTFA framework, FINTRAC's role and the three offences behind suspicious transaction reporting
Describe the five compliance program elements, including the written, ongoing training program and plan and the two-year review
Apply Canadian identity verification, beneficial ownership, PEP, HIO and third-party determination rules
Decide when an STR, large cash report or EFT report is due, meet the deadlines and avoid tipping off
Apply Ministerial directives and sanctions-related reporting, and share information lawfully under section 11.01
Explain FINTRAC's administrative monetary penalties and the 2026 compliance agreement and order regime

quest.name: The Maplecrest Mandate

With CAMLO Nadia Bouchard, investigator Harpreet Sandhu, branch manager Mei Chen, payments head Kwame Mensah and auditor Élise Tremblay, you must make the PCMLTFA work at the counter, in the signal room and in the boardroom.

cards.title: Stage one: the rulebook vault
cards.setting: Financial crime office, Maplecrest Bank head office, King Street West, Toronto. 8:45 am.

lines.text: Your new badge opens the glass door to the bank's financial crime floor. A whiteboard reads: 'FINTRAC exam window opens in 10 weeks.'
Welcome aboard. I'm Nadia Bouchard, Chief Anti-Money Laundering Officer. In Canada the law calls my role the compliance officer, and I answer to FINTRAC for our program.
Harpreet Sandhu, financial intelligence unit. I decide which files become suspicious transaction reports. Spoiler: that is where most banks get fined.
(on video from Richmond, BC) Mei Chen, branch manager. My tellers ask me every week which rules are FINTRAC's and which are OSFI's. I'd love a straight answer.
(from Montréal) Kwame Mensah, payments and correspondent operations. And since March 2026 the penalties have a lot more zeros. My board is nervous.
So your first mission is the map: the Act, the Regulations, who enforces them, which crimes they target and what changed in 2026.
Five stages, then the exam. By the end you should be able to brief a teller, an investigator and a director. Let's open the vault.

cards.title: Canada's AML/ATF rulebook in one minute

scenes.heading: One Act
scenes.narration: The core law is the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act, usually shortened to the PCMLTFA. Banks are reporting entities under it.

scenes.heading: Detailed Regulations
scenes.narration: The Act sets the duties. The Regulations fill in the detail: when to verify identity, what to record, which transactions to report and what a compliance program must contain.

scenes.heading: One supervisor and intelligence unit
scenes.narration: FINTRAC, the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada, receives reports, analyses them and supervises compliance. It can examine a bank and impose penalties.

scenes.heading: Three target crimes
scenes.narration: Reporting duties aim at money laundering, terrorist activity financing and, since 2024, sanctions evasion. Each is defined by reference to other Canadian laws.

scenes.heading: Finance sets policy
scenes.narration: The Minister of Finance owns AML policy and can issue Ministerial directives that require extra measures for transactions linked to high-risk foreign states.

scenes.heading: 2026 brought sharper teeth
scenes.narration: In March 2026 Parliament required programs to be effective, raised penalty ceilings sharply and added compliance agreements and public compliance orders.

cards.title: How the rules stack up
cards.caption: Law at the top, your own procedures at the base. If guidance and law differ, the law wins.

items.label: The PCMLTFA (the Act)
items.detail: Duties in law: keep records, verify identity, report, run a compliance program, follow directives.

items.label: PCMLTF Regulations
items.detail: The detail: thresholds, methods, timing, records and the compliance program elements.

cards.question: Which body receives suspicious transaction reports from Canadian banks and supervises their PCMLTFA compliance?
options: OSFI, the prudential regulator
FINTRAC, the financial intelligence unit
The RCMP's financial crime unit
The Department of Finance
cards.explanation: FINTRAC is both Canada's financial intelligence unit and the AML/ATF supervisor under the PCMLTFA. OSFI supervises prudential soundness; it is not where STRs go.

cards.caption: A simple map of the bodies a compliance team deals with most.

cards.title: Three offences behind every report
cards.body:
Section 7 of the Act ties suspicious transaction reporting to three kinds of offence:

- **Money laundering offence**: dealing with proceeds of crime to conceal or convert them, as defined through the Criminal Code and related laws.
- **Terrorist activity financing offence**: offences in the Criminal Code's terrorism financing provisions, including providing or collecting property for terrorist activity and dealing in property of listed terrorists.
- **Sanctions evasion offence**: added to the reporting duty in 2024. It means breaking a prohibition in a regulation made under the **United Nations Act**, **Part 1 of the Special Economic Measures Act** or the **Sergei Magnitsky Law**.

You never need to prove which offence happened. The reporting test is whether there are reasonable grounds to suspect a link to one of them. Stage four covers that test in detail.

A business covered by section 5 of the Act, such as a bank

An order from the Finance Minister adding measures for a high-risk state
The person appointed to implement the bank's compliance program

cards.title: A turning point at the board
cards.setting: Board risk committee pre-meeting, 40th floor, Toronto.

lines.text: Élise Tremblay, internal audit. I lead our two-year effectiveness review, so I read every FINTRAC penalty notice. The pattern is not subtle.
The board's question is simple. Is a FINTRAC penalty a finding that the bank laundered money?
No. The notices say it plainly: these are administrative violations of the Act and Regulations, not criminal findings. But they are public, and the reputational damage is real.
And the biggest bank penalties all start the same way: suspicious transaction reports that should have been filed and weren't.
Which is why the board wants a briefing on the 2026 changes before Thursday. Who's drafting it?

cards.title: Briefing the board on enforcement
cards.situation: Kwame asks you to draft one line for the board on what a FINTRAC administrative monetary penalty means for Maplecrest. Which line do you send?

choices.text: A penalty is an administrative sanction for breaking the PCMLTFA or its Regulations. It is published, and it is not a criminal conviction for money laundering.
choices.outcome: Exactly how FINTRAC describes it in its public notices. It is accurate and still makes clear that the reputational cost is serious.

choices.text: A penalty means FINTRAC has found that the bank was used to launder money and has referred it for prosecution.
choices.outcome: Wrong. A penalty concerns compliance failures. Proceeding by violation and by offence are alternatives under the Act, and FINTRAC's notices stress that penalties are not criminal findings.

choices.text: A penalty is a confidential supervisory matter that only the bank and FINTRAC will know about.
choices.outcome: Wrong. The Act requires FINTRAC to make public the nature of the violation, the name and the amount once a violation is established.

choices.text: A penalty is mostly a cost of doing business; paying quickly ends all further obligations.
choices.outcome: Partly true that paying ends the proceedings on that notice, but since 2026 the Act also requires a compliance agreement afterwards, and ignoring it leads to a public compliance order.

cards.front: Myth: OSFI is where a bank files its STRs.
cards.back: Fact: suspicious transaction reports go to FINTRAC. OSFI is the prudential supervisor of federally regulated banks.

cards.front: Myth: an employee is personally responsible for the bank's PCMLTFA compliance.
cards.back: Fact: the Regulations make the employer, not the employee, responsible for compliance. Staff still have to follow the bank's procedures.

cards.front: Myth: sanctions are only Global Affairs Canada's problem.
cards.back: Fact: since 2024, suspected sanctions evasion must be reported to FINTRAC through an STR.

cards.front: Myth: FINTRAC guidance is the law.
cards.back: Fact: the Act and Regulations are the law. Guidance shows how FINTRAC interprets them and what examiners expect.
Fact: the Act requires FINTRAC to publish the name, the nature of the violation and the amount.

cards.question: Since 2024, which new category of suspicion must Canadian banks report to FINTRAC through a suspicious transaction report?
options: Suspected tax evasion by any client
Suspected sanctions evasion
Suspected consumer fraud against the bank
Suspected breaches of privacy law
cards.explanation: Section 7(c) of the PCMLTFA now covers transactions linked to a sanctions evasion offence under the UN Act, SEMA or the Magnitsky Law. Fraud or tax crime may still lead to an STR, but only through a money laundering link.

cards.title: Real case: The Toronto-Dominion Bank (FINTRAC, 2024)
cards.body:
On 9 April 2024 FINTRAC imposed an administrative monetary penalty of **CAD 9,185,000** on The Toronto-Dominion Bank for **five violations** found in a 2023 compliance examination.

According to FINTRAC's public notice:

- The bank did not file **20 suspicious transaction reports** out of 178 case files reviewed.
- It did not identify its full high-risk client population: **96 clients** were missing from its high-risk program.
- High-risk clients went without the special measures the Regulations require, and enhanced measures under a **Ministerial directive** were not applied to 11 clients.
- Ongoing monitoring and the records of those measures fell short.

FINTRAC stressed that the penalty was for administrative violations, not criminal money laundering offences. The lesson for you: one weak link, here client risk rating, can cascade into four other violations.

cards.title: Real case: Royal Bank of Canada (FINTRAC, 2023)
cards.body:
On 3 November 2023 FINTRAC imposed a penalty of **CAD 7,475,000** on Royal Bank of Canada for **three violations** found in a 2022 examination.

The public notice describes:

- **16 suspicious transaction reports** not filed out of 130 files reviewed, including files where the bank had been served with **production orders** but did not escalate them for an STR decision.
- STRs that bundled transactions from several branch locations into one report, contrary to FINTRAC's reporting instructions.
- Policies that pointed staff to **reasonable grounds to believe**, a higher bar than the legal test of **reasonable grounds to suspect**.

The lesson: a single wrong word in a procedure can quietly raise the reporting threshold across a whole bank.

cards.title: Stage one take-aways
items: The PCMLTFA and its Regulations are the core of Canada's AML/ATF regime for banks.
FINTRAC receives reports, supervises compliance and imposes administrative monetary penalties.
Reporting targets money laundering, terrorist activity financing and, since 2024, sanctions evasion.
The Finance Minister can issue directives for high-risk states; Russia, Iran and the DPRK are in force.
Since 26 March 2026, programs must be reasonably designed, risk-based and effective, and penalties are far higher.
Penalties are administrative, not criminal convictions, but they are published.

cards.prompt: Think about your own role at a Canadian bank. Which of the three target offences are you most likely to meet, and who in your bank decides whether a report goes to FINTRAC?

quiz.question: What is the main federal statute that sets AML/ATF duties for Canadian banks?
options: The Bank Act, through its Financial Consumer Protection Framework provisions
The Special Economic Measures Act
The Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act
The Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act
quiz.explanation: The PCMLTFA sets record-keeping, identity, reporting and compliance program duties. The other laws matter, but none is the core AML statute.

quiz.question: A teller at Maplecrest asks where suspicious transaction reports are sent. What is the correct answer?
options: To FINTRAC, Canada's financial intelligence unit
To OSFI, which supervises the bank's prudential soundness
To the local police service that covers the branch's area
To Global Affairs Canada if any foreign party is involved
quiz.explanation: STRs go to FINTRAC. OSFI is the prudential regulator, and police receive FINTRAC disclosures, not the bank's STRs.

quiz.question: Which three kinds of offence does the section 7 suspicious transaction duty now cover?
options: Money laundering, tax evasion and securities fraud
Money laundering, terrorist activity financing and sanctions evasion
Terrorist financing, bribery and insider trading
Sanctions evasion, cybercrime and identity theft
quiz.explanation: Section 7(a)-(c) names money laundering, terrorist activity financing and, since 2024, sanctions evasion offences.

quiz.question: A client wires funds that appear designed to get around a SEMA asset freeze on a listed Russian company. Under the PCMLTFA, how is this best described?
options: A matter only for Global Affairs Canada, outside the PCMLTFA entirely
A terrorist financing offence because sanctions are involved
A breach of the bank's privacy obligations under PIPEDA
A possible sanctions evasion offence that can lead to an STR
quiz.explanation: A sanctions evasion offence means breaching a prohibition under the UN Act, Part 1 of SEMA or the Magnitsky Law, and section 7(c) requires an STR where there are reasonable grounds to suspect it.

quiz.question: Who issues Ministerial directives under Part 1.1 of the PCMLTFA?
options: The Director of FINTRAC
The Superintendent of Financial Institutions
The Minister of Finance
The Minister of Foreign Affairs
quiz.explanation: Directives are issued by the Minister of Finance. FINTRAC informs reporting entities, explains them and examines compliance with them.

quiz.question: Kwame's board asks what the 2026 amendment to subsection 9.6 added. Which answer is accurate?
options: Banks must now file STRs within three business days
Compliance officers must be approved by FINTRAC
Training must be delivered to every employee at least once every quarter
The program must be reasonably designed, risk-based and effective
quiz.explanation: New subsection 9.6(1.1), in force 26 March 2026, requires the program to be reasonably designed, risk-based and effective. The other options are invented.

quiz.question: A director says FINTRAC's 2024 penalty on TD proves the bank committed money laundering. How should you respond?
options: That is correct, because FINTRAC penalties always follow criminal convictions
That is correct, because only laundering cases are published
The penalty related only to privacy breaches, not AML
FINTRAC said it was for administrative violations, not criminal offences
quiz.explanation: FINTRAC's notice says the penalty was for administrative violations of the Act and Regulations, not for criminal money laundering or terrorist financing offences.

quiz.question: Which statement about FINTRAC guidance is correct?
options: It overrides the Regulations whenever the two of them are in conflict with each other
It applies only to money services businesses, not banks
It shows FINTRAC's interpretation; the Act and Regulations are binding
It is optional reading with no role in examinations
quiz.explanation: Guidance shows FINTRAC's interpretation and expectations, which examiners use, but the legal obligations come from the Act and Regulations.

quiz.question: In RBC's 2023 penalty, FINTRAC criticised policies that referred to 'reasonable grounds to believe'. Why was that a problem?
options: It set a higher bar than the legal test of reasonable grounds to suspect
It set a lower bar than the legal test, which caused far too many reports to be filed
It copied wording from the Criminal Code without permission
It applied only to terrorist financing and not to laundering
quiz.explanation: The STR test is reasonable grounds to suspect. Pointing staff to reasonable grounds to believe raises the threshold and leads to missed reports.

quiz.question: Which set of Ministerial directives is in force according to FINTRAC's directives page?
options: Russia, Belarus and Myanmar
Iran, Syria and Afghanistan
The DPRK, Venezuela and Russia
Russia, Iran and the DPRK
quiz.explanation: FINTRAC lists three directives in force: Russia (2024), Iran (2020) and the DPRK (2017).

sessions.title: The compliance program, training plan and effectiveness review
sessions.summary: Build the five compliance program elements in section 156, including the written ongoing training program and plan, the risk assessment, new technology reviews and the two-year effectiveness review.
objectives: List the compliance program elements in section 156 of the Regulations
Describe what FINTRAC expects in a training program and training plan
Apply the risk assessment factors and the pre-launch rule for new technologies
Explain the two-year effectiveness review and reporting to a senior officer

cards.title: Stage two: the program forge
cards.setting: Nadia's office, Toronto. A FINTRAC examination notice sits on the desk.

lines.text: FINTRAC's notice asks for our compliance program documents. Everything starts with section 9.6 of the Act and section 156 of the Regulations.
And since March 2026, 'we have a binder' is not enough. The Act now says the program must be reasonably designed, risk-based and effective.
Effective means examiners will test outcomes: did we actually catch and report what we should have?
From the branch side, the bit I own is training. My new teller started Monday. Is she covered by the training rules from day one?
Good question, and the answer lives in our training plan. Let's build the program piece by piece so you can answer FINTRAC's first request.

cards.title: The compliance program, element by element

scenes.heading: Someone in charge
scenes.narration: The bank must appoint a person responsible for implementing the program. At a large bank this is usually the Chief Anti-Money Laundering Officer, supported by a dedicated team.

scenes.heading: Written policies
scenes.narration: Policies and procedures must be written, kept up to date and, for an entity, approved by a senior officer. They turn the law into steps staff can follow.

scenes.heading: A documented risk assessment
scenes.narration: The bank assesses and documents its money laundering and terrorist financing risk, looking at clients, products, channels, geography, affiliates and any other relevant factor.

scenes.heading: Training program and plan
scenes.narration: Paragraphs 156(1)(d) and (e) require a written, ongoing compliance training program for employees and agents, plus a documented plan for delivering it.

scenes.heading: Two-year effectiveness review
scenes.narration: An auditor tests the program at least every two years, and the findings go to a senior officer in writing within 30 days of completing the review.

cards.title: The five elements as a living cycle
cards.caption: FINTRAC describes these as the elements every reporting entity must implement under section 156 of the Regulations.

items.label: Compliance officer
items.detail: Owns implementation and reports to senior management.

items.label: Policies and procedures
items.detail: Written, current and approved by a senior officer.

items.label: Risk assessment
items.detail: Documented view of ML/TF risk across the business.

items.label: Training program and plan
items.detail: Written, ongoing, delivered to the right people.

items.label: Effectiveness review
items.detail: Tested every two years; findings drive the next update.

cards.question: Which pair of provisions requires a written, ongoing compliance training program and a documented plan to deliver it?
options: Section 7 and section 8 of the Act
Paragraphs 156(1)(d) and (e) of the Regulations
Section 123.1 of the Regulations
Part 1.1 of the Act
cards.explanation: Paragraph 156(1)(d) requires the written, ongoing training program; paragraph 156(1)(e) requires a documented plan and delivery of the training.

cards.title: Risk factors the assessment must weigh
cards.caption: Paragraph 156(1)(c) lists these factors. New technologies or developments must be assessed before launch (subsection 156(2)).

items.label: Clients and relationships
items.detail: Including business and correspondent banking relationships.

items.label: Products, services, channels
items.detail: How clients reach you: branch, online, agents, cards.

items.label: Geography
items.detail: Where the bank and its clients operate and transact.

items.label: Affiliates and other factors
items.detail: Risks from affiliated entities, plus anything else relevant.

cards.title: What a good training program contains
Program element or not?
cards.prompt: Sort each item: is it one of the compliance program elements in section 156, or something else?

items.text: Appointing the person responsible for the program
Senior-officer-approved written policies
A documented ML/TF risk assessment
A written, ongoing training program and plan
A two-year effectiveness review plan
Filing a large cash transaction report
Quarterly approval of each STR by the board
Registering the bank as a money services business

cards.title: The new-product question
cards.setting: Product committee, Toronto. Kwame presents a pilot.

lines.text: We want to launch instant cross-border payouts through a fintech partner's app next quarter. Marketing has the launch date already.
Then we have a regulatory step first. Subsection 156(2) says new developments and new technologies get a documented risk assessment before we introduce them.
Before? Not after we see how it performs?
Before. And I will test whether that assessment existed when I do the effectiveness review.

cards.title: Launching the payout app
cards.situation: The fintech payout pilot is scheduled to go live in six weeks. No ML/TF risk assessment has been documented yet. What should Kwame do?

choices.text: Document an ML/TF risk assessment of the new channel and product before launch, and update controls and training to match.
choices.outcome: Correct. Subsection 156(2) requires the assessment before introducing a new technology or development, and the result should feed monitoring, policies and training.

choices.text: Launch on time and run the risk assessment at the next annual review cycle.
choices.outcome: This breaches subsection 156(2), which requires the assessment before the change. An examiner would treat it as a program gap.

choices.text: Ask the fintech partner to confirm in writing that the app is low risk.
choices.outcome: A partner's comfort letter may be useful input, but the bank itself must assess and document the risk.

choices.text: Launch for staff accounts only and assess the risk once external clients join.
choices.outcome: Better than a full launch, but it still introduces the technology before the documented assessment the Regulations require.

cards.title: Running the two-year effectiveness review
cards.prompt: Put the steps of the effectiveness review in a sensible order.
steps: Document a plan for reviewing the compliance program
Have an internal or external auditor test the program's effectiveness
Document the findings of the review
Report findings, policy updates and implementation status to a senior officer within 30 days
Track remediation and feed lessons into policies, risk assessment and training

cards.back: The 2026 test in subsection 9.6(1.1): the program must fit the bank's risks and must actually work, not just exist on paper.
Policies and procedures of an entity must be approved by a senior officer, not only by the compliance team.
Section 157: written policies for enhanced identity checks and other enhanced steps, such as more frequent updates and monitoring, for high-risk clients.
The documented plan covering who is trained, on what, how and how often, and how delivery is recorded.
A test of the whole program every two years by an auditor, or by the entity itself if it has no auditor.

cards.question: Within what time must an entity report the findings of its two-year effectiveness review to a senior officer?
options: Within 30 days after the review is completed
Within 5 working days after the review starts
Within 90 days after the year end
Only when FINTRAC requests it
cards.explanation: Subsection 156(4) requires a written report of the findings, policy updates and implementation status to a senior officer within 30 days after the review is completed.

cards.title: Real case: Exchange Bank of Canada (FINTRAC, 2024)
cards.body:
On 5 November 2024 FINTRAC imposed a penalty of **CAD 2,457,750** on Exchange Bank of Canada for **three violations** found in an examination between December 2022 and April 2024. FINTRAC said the bank had not built an **effective compliance program for its business model and global reach**, with gaps in oversight by its chief AML officer, transaction monitoring, investigations and ongoing monitoring of high-risk clients.

The notice lists **5 missed STRs out of 26 files**, about 20%, and a monitoring system that did not cover all products, did not flag volume swings well and lacked enough ML/TF indicators, linked to weak testing and tuning.

The bank appealed. On **18 December 2025 the Federal Court confirmed the violations** and varied the penalty to **CAD 1,027,975**. The lesson: the right of appeal exists, but the findings on program design stood.

Stage two take-aways
items: Section 9.6 of the Act and section 156 of the Regulations set the compliance program.
The elements: compliance officer, approved written policies, documented risk assessment, written ongoing training program and plan, two-year effectiveness review.
Since 26 March 2026, the program must be reasonably designed, risk-based and effective.
Assess and document the risk of a new technology or development before launch.
Review findings go to a senior officer in writing within 30 days of completing the review.
High-risk clients need the special measures in section 157 of the Regulations.

cards.prompt: Look at your bank's AML training plan, or imagine one for your team. Does it name who is trained, on which topics, by which method and how often? What would an examiner see as missing?

quiz.question: Which provision requires a Canadian reporting entity to establish and implement a compliance program?
options: Section 7 of the PCMLTFA
Section 148 of the Regulations
Subsection 9.6(1) of the PCMLTFA
Section 11.01 of the PCMLTFA
quiz.explanation: Subsection 9.6(1) requires the program; section 156 of the Regulations sets out how it is implemented.

quiz.question: Who must approve an entity's written compliance policies and procedures under paragraph 156(1)(b)?
options: FINTRAC's compliance branch
A senior officer of the entity
The bank's external auditor
Each branch manager for their own branch
quiz.explanation: The Regulations require written policies kept up to date and, for an entity, approved by a senior officer.

quiz.question: Mei's branch hires three tellers. Under paragraphs 156(1)(d) and (e), what must the bank have in place for them?
options: A written, ongoing training program and a documented delivery plan
A one-off certificate issued by FINTRAC before they are allowed to serve any clients
An annual exam set and marked by OSFI
A signed statement that they have read the Act
quiz.explanation: The Regulations require a written, ongoing training program for employees and agents, plus a documented plan and delivery. FINTRAC does not certify individual tellers.

quiz.question: Which item does FINTRAC say a training plan should cover?
options: Each employee's salary band and bonus targets
Recipients, topics and materials, delivery methods and frequency
The names of clients reported in STRs
The bank's capital ratios, liquidity buffers and stress-testing results
quiz.explanation: FINTRAC's guidance says the plan should set out who is trained, on what, how and how often, and the bank should keep records of delivery.

quiz.question: Maplecrest plans to launch a new digital onboarding app. When must the ML/TF risk of the app be assessed and documented?
options: Within 30 days after launch
At the next two-year effectiveness review
Only if FINTRAC asks for it
Before the app is introduced
quiz.explanation: Subsection 156(2) requires the assessment before carrying out a new development or introducing a new technology.

quiz.question: Which factor is NOT one of those listed in paragraph 156(1)(c) for the risk assessment?
options: Clients, business relationships and correspondent relationships
Products, services and delivery channels
The personal credit scores of the bank's employees
The geographic location of the bank's activities
quiz.explanation: The listed factors are clients and relationships, products, services and channels, geography, affiliates and any other relevant factor. Staff credit scores are not among them.

quiz.question: Who carries out the two-year effectiveness review at a bank that has an internal audit function?
options: FINTRAC examiners
The bank's compliance officer acting alone, without any auditor
A committee of front-line staff
An internal or external auditor of the bank
quiz.explanation: Subsection 156(3) requires the review by an internal or external auditor; the entity itself may do it only if it has no auditor.

quiz.question: Élise finished the effectiveness review on 1 June. By when must the written report go to a senior officer?
options: Within 30 days after 1 June
Within 15 days after 1 June
Within 90 days after 1 June
By the end of the next financial year
quiz.explanation: Subsection 156(4) sets 30 days after the review is completed for reporting findings, updates and implementation status to a senior officer.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the special measures in section 157 of the Regulations?
options: An automatic exit of every client rated high risk within 30 days
A requirement to report every high-risk client to FINTRAC in a monthly list with a summary of their activity
A ban on opening accounts for any non-resident
Written policies for enhanced identity checks, more frequent updates and closer monitoring
quiz.explanation: Section 157 requires written policies for enhanced verification and other enhanced mitigation, including more frequent updating and ongoing monitoring at a risk-appropriate frequency.

quiz.question: In the Exchange Bank of Canada case, what did the Federal Court decide in December 2025?
options: It overturned all violations and cancelled the penalty
It confirmed the violations and varied the penalty amount
It sent the whole case back to FINTRAC for a fresh examination of the bank
It converted the penalty into a criminal charge
quiz.explanation: FINTRAC's notice records that the Federal Court confirmed the violations and varied the penalty to CAD 1,027,975.

sessions.title: Know your client: identity, beneficial ownership, PEPs and third parties
sessions.summary: Verify identity using the prescribed methods, collect and confirm beneficial ownership, apply PEP and HIO rules, make third-party determinations and keep monitoring relationships.
objectives: Apply identity verification triggers and methods for persons
Collect and confirm beneficial ownership and report registry discrepancies
Distinguish foreign PEPs, domestic PEPs and HIOs and apply the right measures
Make and record third-party determinations and set ongoing monitoring

cards.title: Stage three: the onboarding gate
cards.setting: Maplecrest Bank, No. 3 Road branch, Richmond, BC. 10:15 am.

lines.text: Busy morning. A numbered company wants a business account, a walk-in wants to wire CAD 1,500 to Manila, and a client's nephew is depositing cash 'for his uncle'.
(on video) Three classic know-your-client moments: identity, beneficial ownership and third-party determination. Let's take them one at a time.
The numbered company says its owner prefers to stay private. Can we open the account anyway?
We can't open an anonymous account, and for an entity we must collect who owns or controls it. Privacy preferences don't change the Regulations.
And the account opening form says the director is an ambassador's daughter. That's a PEP question too.
Okay. Teach me the gate, then.

cards.title: Know your client, the Canadian way

scenes.heading: Verify identity
scenes.narration: At account opening, and for certain non-account transactions, the bank verifies identity using a method set out in the Regulations, such as government photo ID, a credit file or the dual-process method.

scenes.heading: Look through entities
scenes.narration: For a corporation, the bank collects the names of directors and of everyone who owns or controls 25% or more, plus the ownership, control and structure, and takes reasonable measures to confirm it.

scenes.heading: Ask the PEP question
scenes.narration: The bank determines whether a client is a foreign or domestic politically exposed person, a head of an international organization, or a family member or close associate.

scenes.heading: Spot the third party
scenes.narration: When opening an account, or receiving CAD 10,000 or more in cash, the bank takes reasonable measures to find out whether someone else is behind the client.

scenes.heading: Keep watching
scenes.narration: Throughout the relationship, ongoing monitoring keeps information current, reassesses risk and checks that activity fits what the bank knows.

cards.title: Accepted ways to verify a person's identity (section 105)
cards.caption: Wording simplified. Follow your bank's procedures for the exact checks and records.

items.label: Government photo ID
items.detail: Valid federal, provincial or foreign government photo ID; confirm name and photo match the person.

items.label: Credit file
items.detail: A Canadian credit file at least three years old, from more than one source; confirm name, address and date of birth.

items.label: Dual-process
items.detail: Two different reliable sources confirming two of: name and address, name and date of birth, name and an account.

items.label: Other prescribed methods
items.detail: Such as reliance on another entity or an agent, under the conditions the Regulations set.

cards.question: A walk-in, non-account client asks Mei's branch to send an international wire of CAD 1,500. Must the bank verify the person's identity?
options: No, only account holders are ever verified
Yes, international EFT requests of CAD 1,000 or more trigger verification
Only if the amount reaches CAD 10,000
Only if the destination is under a Ministerial directive
cards.explanation: Section 86 of the Regulations requires a financial entity to verify the identity of a person who requests an international EFT of CAD 1,000 or more. A directive country would add more measures, but the CAD 1,000 trigger applies anyway.

cards.title: Beneficial ownership, step by step
cards.body:
When it verifies an entity, the bank must obtain (section 138):

- **Corporations:** names of all directors, and names and addresses of everyone who owns or controls, directly or indirectly, **25% or more** of the shares.
- **Trusts:** names and addresses of all trustees and all known beneficiaries and settlors.
- **Other entities:** names and addresses of everyone who owns or controls 25% or more.
- **In all cases:** information establishing ownership, control and structure.

The bank takes **reasonable measures to confirm** the information when first obtained and during ongoing monitoring, and keeps a record. If it **cannot** obtain or confirm it, it must take reasonable measures to verify the identity of the **chief executive officer** (or equivalent) and apply **special measures**.

For federally incorporated corporations, a **material discrepancy** with the public federal registry must be reported to the Director under the Canada Business Corporations Act **within 30 days**, unless it is resolved within that time.

cards.title: Who counts as what?
cards.prompt: Match each person to the right Canadian category.

pairs.left: A serving minister in a foreign government
The head of an organization set up by governments of states
A known business partner of a foreign ambassador
pairs.right: Close associate of a politically exposed foreign person

pairs.left: The president of a foreign state-owned bank

cards.title: PEP measures for account holders (section 121)
cards.caption: The bank must also make the PEP determination for international EFTs of CAD 100,000 or more (section 116).

items.label: Who
items.left: Foreign PEP, family member or close associate
items.right: Domestic PEP or HIO, family or associate

items.label: When measures apply
items.right: Only if the bank assesses high ML/TF risk

items.label: Approval
items.left: Senior management approval to keep the account open

lines.text: A young man places a thick envelope on the counter: CAD 12,400 in fifties and hundreds.
He says it's for his uncle's account, and he is not on that account.
That is a third-party determination under section 134, and the amount is over the CAD 10,000 large cash line, so there is a report too.
And if he insists it's his own money but everything says otherwise?
Then we record what he told us and why we have reasonable grounds to suspect a third party. And we ask whether this belongs with my team as unusual activity.

cards.title: Cash for 'my uncle'
cards.situation: The young man deposits CAD 12,400 in cash into his uncle's account. He first says it is his uncle's money, then says it is his own savings. He will not give his uncle's occupation. What should the teller do?

choices.text: Take the deposit, record his statement and the grounds to suspect a third party, make sure the large cash report is captured, and escalate internally.
choices.outcome: Best answer. Section 134 requires the third-party record when the bank cannot determine but has reasonable grounds to suspect; the cash triggers a large cash report; and the shifting story is an indicator for the FIU to assess for an STR.

choices.text: Refuse the deposit and tell him the bank suspects money laundering.
choices.outcome: Refusing may be a business choice, but telling him about suspicion risks tipping off and does not replace the recording and escalation duties.

choices.text: Accept the deposit as his own money because he said so in the end.
choices.outcome: The Regulations require reasonable measures, not blind acceptance. Where grounds to suspect a third party remain, the bank must record them.

choices.text: Accept the deposit, file nothing now, and ask the uncle to call the branch next week.
choices.outcome: Following up with the account holder can help, but the large cash report and third-party record arise at the time of the transaction.

cards.title: Which duty does it trigger?
cards.prompt: Sort each situation into the main know-your-client duty it raises.

items.text: A person opens a personal chequing account
A walk-in asks to buy a CAD 3,500 money order
A numbered company opens a business account
A family trust names three beneficiaries
Corporate registry shows a different 25% owner than the client declared
Someone deposits CAD 11,000 cash into another person's account
A new account will be used by the client's employer

cards.title: Opening an account for a corporation
cards.prompt: Put the onboarding steps for a corporate client in a sensible order.
steps: Confirm the corporation's existence and verify its identity
Collect the names of directors and of owners or controllers of 25% or more
Obtain information on ownership, control and structure
Take reasonable measures to confirm the beneficial ownership information
Determine whether any relevant person is a PEP, HIO, family member or close associate
Assess the client's ML/TF risk and apply special measures if high
Set the ongoing monitoring frequency based on that risk

cards.question: Maplecrest cannot obtain or confirm the beneficial ownership of a corporate client. What must it do under subsection 138(4)?
options: Close the account immediately and file an STR
Take reasonable measures to verify the CEO's identity and apply special measures
Ask the client to sign a declaration and take no further step
Report the client to Corporations Canada within 5 days
cards.explanation: Subsection 138(4) requires reasonable measures to verify the identity of the CEO (or person in that function) and the special measures in section 157. An STR is required only if there are reasonable grounds to suspect.

cards.title: Common onboarding mistakes
cards.body:
- **Stopping at the 25% line.** You also need control and structure, and must try to confirm them.
- **Forgetting family and associates.** The PEP determination covers them too.
- **Forgetting the five-year rule.** Domestic PEP and HIO status lasts five years after leaving office; foreign PEP status never lapses.
- **Treating every domestic PEP as high risk.** Extra measures follow your risk assessment; for foreign PEPs they always apply.
- **Leaving the third-party box blank.** If you cannot determine but suspect, record why.

cards.title: Real case: a foreign PEP without source of wealth (TD, 2024)
cards.body:
FINTRAC's 2024 notice on The Toronto-Dominion Bank describes a **politically exposed foreign person** who was allowed to transact for **more than two years** without the bank obtaining the required details, including **source of funds, source of wealth** and the nature and purpose of transactions.

The same notice found that **96 clients** were never entered into the bank's high-risk program because of weaknesses in its client risk rating tools during a system transition, so **85** of them received no special measures at all.

For onboarding teams, the lesson is that a PEP flag or a high-risk rating is not a label. It is a trigger for specific steps the Regulations require, and the bank must be able to show they happened.

cards.title: Real case: special measures not applied (FNBC, 2025)
cards.body:
FINTRAC's 2025 notice on First Nations Bank of Canada found **six high-risk clients** in the sample who received **none of the special measures** the Regulations require. The bank ran alert-based transaction monitoring, but FINTRAC did not see ongoing monitoring of high-risk clients that matched their risk level.

A separate violation recorded **five instances** where the bank did not reassess client risk ratings or keep client information up to date, against its own policy.

The lesson for front-line and onboarding staff: enhanced measures must be **visible in the file**. If a client is high risk, the record should show the extra identity checks, the more frequent updates and the closer monitoring.

cards.title: Stage three take-aways
items: Verify identity using a method in section 105; international EFTs of CAD 1,000 or more trigger it for non-account clients.
No anonymous accounts: if identity cannot be verified, the account is not opened.
Entities: collect directors, 25%+ owners or controllers, trust parties and structure, and try to confirm them.
Federal registry discrepancies go to the CBCA Director within 30 days unless resolved.
Foreign PEPs always need source of funds and wealth, senior approval and special measures; domestic PEPs and HIOs need them when high risk.
Third-party determination applies at account opening and to cash of CAD 10,000 or more.

cards.prompt: Recall the last unusual onboarding you saw or heard about. Which of today's checks (identity, beneficial ownership, PEP, third party) would have helped most, and how would you document it?

quiz.question: Which of these is an accepted method in section 105 to verify a person's identity?
options: A selfie emailed by the client with no other check
Valid government-issued photo ID, checking name and photo match the person
A utility bill alone, without any second source
A verbal confirmation from a long-serving colleague who says they have known the client for years
quiz.explanation: Section 105 lists government photo ID, credit file, dual-process and other prescribed methods. A single utility bill or an informal confirmation is not enough.

quiz.question: Under the credit file method, how old must the Canadian credit file be?
options: At least three years
At least six months
At least one year
At least ten years
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 105(1)(c) requires a credit file located in Canada that has existed for at least three years and draws on more than one source.

quiz.question: For a corporate client, what ownership level triggers collection of an owner's name and address under section 138?
options: Owning or controlling, directly or indirectly, 25% or more
Owning 10% or more of the voting shares, held directly in the owner's own name only
Owning more than 50% of the shares
Holding any shares at all, however small
quiz.explanation: Section 138 sets the line at 25% or more, held directly or indirectly, and also requires all directors' names.

quiz.question: Maplecrest finds a material discrepancy between the beneficial owners a CBCA corporation declared and the federal registry. What does section 138.1 require?
options: Report it to FINTRAC as a suspicious transaction report within 24 hours of finding it
Close the account and notify the client in writing
Report it to the CBCA Director within 30 days unless resolved
Ignore it if the client says the registry is out of date
quiz.explanation: Section 138.1 requires a discrepancy report to the Director under the Canada Business Corporations Act within 30 days, unless the discrepancy is resolved within that period.

quiz.question: A new account holder is a former ambassador of another country who left office many years ago. How does the Act treat this person?
options: No longer a PEP because they left office
Still a foreign PEP: that definition has no end date
A politically exposed domestic person, because the person now lives permanently in Canada
A head of an international organization
quiz.explanation: The Act defines a politically exposed foreign person as someone who holds or has held the listed offices, with no prescribed period. Domestic PEP and HIO status, by contrast, lasts only for the prescribed period, which section 2 of the Regulations sets at five years.

quiz.question: The bank determines that a new account holder is a domestic PEP. Its risk assessment rates the client as low risk. What does section 121 require?
options: Normal measures; the extra PEP steps apply only if risk is high
Senior management approval and source of wealth checks in every case, whatever the risk rating says
Refusal of the account because domestic PEPs are prohibited
A report to FINTRAC that a domestic PEP has opened an account
quiz.explanation: For domestic PEPs and HIOs (and their family or associates), the source of funds and wealth, senior approval and special measures apply when the bank considers the risk high.

quiz.question: Which three steps apply to an account held by a politically exposed foreign person?
options: Source of funds and wealth, senior management approval, special measures
File a monthly STR, freeze the account, notify Global Affairs
Collect two photo IDs, call the embassy to confirm the client's role, and close the account within a year
Notify the client's government, cap deposits, block wires
quiz.explanation: Subsection 121(1) sets these three measures for foreign PEPs, their family members and close associates who are account holders.

quiz.question: A man deposits CAD 10,500 cash and you cannot tell whether he acts for someone else, but there are reasonable grounds to suspect he does. What must you record?
options: Nothing, because the third party could not be identified by name, address or date of birth
Only the cash amount and his account number
His employer's name and his salary
What he says about acting for himself, and the grounds to suspect
quiz.explanation: Subsection 134(3) requires a record of what the person said about acting on their own behalf and a description of the reasonable grounds to suspect a third party.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of ongoing monitoring under section 123.1 of the Regulations?
options: Detect reportable transactions, keep information current, reassess risk and check activity fits the client
Confirm that clients pay their fees on time
Decide each client's credit limit for the year
Collect marketing consent for new products
quiz.explanation: Section 123.1 lists four purposes: detecting reportable transactions, keeping identity and beneficial ownership information current, reassessing risk and checking consistency with what the bank knows.

quiz.question: What transaction size triggers the PEP determination for a person who asks a bank to initiate an international EFT?
options: CAD 1,000 or more
CAD 10,000 or more
CAD 100,000 or more
CAD 50,000 or more
quiz.explanation: Section 116 requires reasonable measures to determine PEP or HIO status for a person who requests an international EFT of CAD 100,000 or more, and for the beneficiary of one.

sessions.title: STRs, large cash and EFT reports, records and information sharing
sessions.summary: Decide when reasonable grounds to suspect exist, file STRs as soon as practicable without tipping off, meet cash and EFT reporting deadlines, keep records and share information lawfully.
objectives: Apply the reasonable grounds to suspect threshold, including for attempted transactions
Meet large cash and EFT report thresholds, the 24-hour rule and deadlines
Keep and produce records within the required periods
Use section 11.01 information sharing within its conditions

cards.title: Stage four: the signal room
cards.setting: Financial intelligence unit, Maplecrest Bank, Toronto. 2:10 pm.

lines.text: Welcome to the signal room. Every alert, branch referral and production order lands here. My job is to decide: is there reasonable grounds to suspect?
A screen shows a branch referral from Richmond: the cash deposit for 'the uncle', plus three similar deposits at other branches this month.
Pattern across branches, cash just above and below CAD 10,000, a shifting story. I don't need proof of a crime. I need reasonable grounds to suspect.
And separately my team owes FINTRAC electronic funds transfer reports on yesterday's international wires. Different clock, different rules.
Today you learn every report, every clock and the one thing you must never say to a client.

scenes.heading: Simple suspicion
scenes.narration: A gut feeling that something is off, with no facts yet. It is a cue to look closer, not yet the reporting threshold.

scenes.heading: Reasonable grounds to suspect
scenes.narration: Facts, context and indicators that make a link to money laundering, terrorist financing or sanctions evasion a real possibility. This is the STR threshold. You do not need to prove the offence.

scenes.heading: Not 'reasonable grounds to believe'
scenes.narration: Believing is a higher bar than the law sets for STRs. Writing it into bank procedures, as one big bank's policies did, causes missed reports.

scenes.heading: As soon as practicable
scenes.narration: Once the bank's measures establish reasonable grounds to suspect, the STR must be completed and sent as a priority. There is no money threshold.

scenes.heading: No tipping off
scenes.narration: Section 8 makes it an offence to disclose that a report was made, or its contents, with intent to prejudice a criminal investigation.

cards.title: How a signal becomes an STR
cards.caption: FINTRAC's notices show banks failing in the middle steps: closing files without checking indicators.

items.label: Signals
items.detail: Alerts, branch referrals, production orders, negative news, directive hits.

items.label: Triage
items.detail: Is there anything unusual about the client or transaction?

items.label: Investigation
items.detail: Review all relevant accounts and transactions against ML/TF indicators.

items.label: Reasonable grounds to suspect?
items.detail: Facts, context and indicators support a possible link to an offence.

items.label: STR to FINTRAC
items.detail: Filed as soon as practicable, including attempted transactions.

cards.question: Which threshold must be reached before a Canadian bank files a suspicious transaction report?
options: Proof beyond reasonable doubt
Reasonable grounds to believe
Reasonable grounds to suspect
A police request for information
cards.explanation: FINTRAC's guidance describes reasonable grounds to suspect as a step above simple suspicion and below reasonable grounds to believe. You do not need to verify the facts or prove an offence.

cards.title: Prescribed reports at a glance
cards.caption: Thresholds and deadlines from sections 7 and 132 of the Regulations and section 7.1 of the Act.

items.label: Suspicious transaction report
items.left: Reasonable grounds to suspect; any amount; attempted too

items.label: Large cash transaction report
items.left: Cash of CAD 10,000 or more received

items.label: EFT report
items.left: International EFT of CAD 10,000 or more, sent or finally received

items.label: Terrorist or listed person property report
items.left: When a disclosure is required under the Criminal Code or sanctions laws

cards.title: The 24-hour rule and record keeping
Which report, if any?
cards.prompt: Sort each event into the report it triggers at Maplecrest (assume no suspicion unless stated).

items.text: A client deposits CAD 14,000 in cash to a business account
Three cash deposits for the same client total CAD 10,600 within 20 hours
Maplecrest sends a CAD 25,000 wire to Germany at a client's request
Maplecrest is the final recipient of a CAD 18,000 wire from Brazil for a client
A client abandons a CAD 3,000 transfer when asked about its purpose, after a story that does not add up
Indicators suggest a client is routing payments to dodge a SEMA asset freeze
A production order arrives and the client's activity matches ML indicators

lines.text: The young man from yesterday returns with another envelope of cash.
He just asked me straight out: 'Are you reporting me to the government?' My teller froze.
Section 8 targets disclosure with intent to prejudice an investigation, but our policy is stricter: we never confirm or discuss whether a report exists.
Large cash reporting is routine and public knowledge. Anything about suspicion stays inside the bank.

cards.title: 'Are you reporting me?'
cards.situation: The client asks the teller directly whether the bank has reported him to FINTRAC. The FIU is reviewing his activity for an STR. What should the teller say?

choices.text: Explain that the bank follows federal reporting rules for many routine transactions, such as large cash, without discussing his file, and pass the conversation to the branch manager and FIU as procedure requires.
choices.outcome: Best answer. It is truthful about routine reporting, discloses nothing about suspicion or any STR, and keeps the escalation path intact.

choices.text: Reassure him that nothing is wrong and no report has been made.
choices.outcome: This is false and could also become a disclosure about the STR process. Never deny or confirm a suspicious transaction report.

choices.text: Tell him a suspicious transaction report is being considered so he can explain himself.
choices.outcome: This discloses information about an STR and risks prejudicing an investigation. It also falls outside the teller's role.

choices.text: Say nothing at all and refuse to serve him further.
choices.outcome: Avoiding disclosure is right, but abruptly refusing service without following procedure can itself alert him. Escalate through the proper channel.

cards.front: Is there a money threshold for STRs?
cards.back: No. Any amount can be reported, and attempted transactions count too.
As soon as practicable after the bank's measures establish reasonable grounds to suspect; FINTRAC expects it treated as a priority.
FINTRAC's guidance says no one will be prosecuted for sending an STR in good faith.
Within 15 days after receiving the cash (section 132).
Within 5 working days after initiating or finally receiving the transfer (section 132).
At least five years, and records must be producible to FINTRAC within 30 days of a request.

cards.title: Sharing information between reporting entities (section 11.01)
cards.body:
Since 2024, section **11.01** of the Act lets one reporting entity disclose a person's personal information to another **without the person's knowledge or consent**, if:

- the information was collected in the course of its activities;
- the disclosure is reasonable for **detecting or deterring** money laundering, terrorist financing or sanctions evasion;
- asking for consent would risk compromising that purpose; and
- the disclosure follows the Regulations.

The Regulations (Part 8) require a **code of practice approved by the Privacy Commissioner** before relying on this power, and the applicant must notify **FINTRAC** and give it a copy. Anyone who discloses, collects or uses information in **good faith** under section 11.01 is protected from criminal or civil proceedings.

At Maplecrest, staff never share client information with another bank on their own initiative: requests go through the FIU under the approved code.

cards.question: Kwame's team initiated a CAD 40,000 international wire for a client on Monday. By when must the EFT report reach FINTRAC?
options: Within 24 hours
Within 5 working days
Within 15 days
Within 30 days
cards.explanation: Subsection 132(1) requires EFT reports within five working days after the day the bank initiates or finally receives the transfer. Fifteen days applies to large cash reports.

cards.title: Real case: CIBC (FINTRAC, 2023)
cards.body:
On 23 October 2023 FINTRAC imposed a penalty of **CAD 1,329,150** on Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce for **two violations** found in a 2021 examination.

- **A missed STR.** A client had been **arrested and charged** with criminal offences. The bank knew and reviewed the transactions, but decided no report was needed because the activity looked normal for the client's profile, despite ML/TF indicators and the context it held.
- **Unreported EFTs.** In a sample of 20,000 incoming SWIFT payments, FINTRAC found **1,003** international EFTs the bank should have reported as the last Canadian financial institution to receive them, linked to a gap in its process for incomplete name or address data and in its testing.

The lesson: 'normal for this client' does not cancel known context, and reporting systems need testing as much as policies do.

cards.title: Real case: missed STRs at FNBC (FINTRAC, 2025)
Stage four take-aways
items: STR threshold: reasonable grounds to suspect a link to ML, TF or sanctions evasion; no money threshold; attempts count.
File STRs as soon as practicable once your measures establish the threshold.
Never disclose that an STR was made or its contents; section 8 targets disclosure intended to prejudice an investigation.
Large cash: CAD 10,000 or more, within 15 days. International EFTs: CAD 10,000 or more, within 5 working days. The 24-hour rule aggregates.
Keep records at least five years and produce them to FINTRAC within 30 days of a request.
Section 11.01 sharing needs a Privacy Commissioner-approved code of practice.

cards.prompt: Think of a time a client's story changed when you asked a simple question. What would you write in an internal referral so the FIU could judge reasonable grounds to suspect without having to call you back?

quiz.question: Which description best matches 'reasonable grounds to suspect' in FINTRAC's guidance?
options: Above simple suspicion: facts, context or indicators point to a possible offence
Proof that a money laundering offence has occurred
A hunch with no facts or indicators behind it
A police officer's formal belief, backed by evidence, that a crime has definitely been committed
quiz.explanation: FINTRAC places reasonable grounds to suspect above simple suspicion and below reasonable grounds to believe. You do not need to prove or verify an offence.

quiz.question: A client attempts a CAD 2,000 transfer, then cancels it when asked about the purpose, after giving contradictory answers. The FIU finds reasonable grounds to suspect. What applies?
options: No report, because the transaction was not completed
File an STR, because attempted transactions count and there is no money threshold
No report, because it is under CAD 10,000
Only a large cash report, if cash was involved
quiz.explanation: Section 7 covers transactions that occur or are attempted, and FINTRAC confirms there is no monetary threshold for STRs.

quiz.question: When must Maplecrest send an STR?
options: Within 30 days after the first alert is generated, whatever the status of the investigation at that point
At the end of each calendar quarter in a batch
As soon as practicable after its measures establish reasonable grounds to suspect
Only after the client has been told and given a chance to explain
quiz.explanation: FINTRAC's guidance requires STRs as soon as practicable after the bank completes the measures that establish reasonable grounds to suspect, treated as a priority.

quiz.question: Under section 8 of the PCMLTFA, what is prohibited?
options: Any discussion of FINTRAC with clients, including explaining routine large cash and EFT reporting rules
Disclosing an STR or its contents with intent to prejudice an investigation
Filing an STR without first telling the client's lawyer
Sharing STR data with FINTRAC more than once
quiz.explanation: Section 8 bars disclosing that a report was made or its contents with intent to prejudice a criminal investigation, whether or not one has started. Bank policy usually goes further.

quiz.question: A client makes cash deposits of CAD 6,000 at 9 am and CAD 5,000 at 4 pm the same day at two branches of the same bank. The bank knows both are by the same client. What is the effect?
options: Each deposit is under CAD 10,000, so neither of them is reportable to FINTRAC in any form
They count as one cash transaction of CAD 10,000 or more (24-hour rule)
Only the second deposit is reported
They are reportable only if the client is a PEP
quiz.explanation: Section 126 deems cash amounts totalling CAD 10,000 or more within 24 consecutive hours to be one transaction when the bank knows they are by or for the same person or entity, or for the same beneficiary.

quiz.question: What is the deadline for a large cash transaction report?
options: Within 5 working days after the cash is received
As soon as practicable, like an STR
Within 30 days after month end
Within 15 days after the cash is received
quiz.explanation: Subsection 132(3) requires cash reports within 15 days. Five working days applies to EFT reports.

quiz.question: For how long must a bank keep a signature card for an account?
options: At least five years after the day the account is opened
At least two years after the last transaction
At least five years after the day the account is closed
Until FINTRAC's next examination ends
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 148(1)(a) measures the five years from account closure for signature cards, account operating agreements and applications.

quiz.question: Another Canadian bank asks Maplecrest for personal information about a shared client it suspects of laundering. Under section 11.01 and the Regulations, what must be true before Maplecrest shares it without consent?
options: A FINTRAC officer must approve each individual disclosure in advance and in writing, case by case, before any sharing
The client must have been convicted of an offence
It must follow a Privacy Commissioner-approved code of practice and meet section 11.01
Both banks must have filed an STR on the client first
quiz.explanation: Section 11.01 sets the conditions, and Part 8 of the Regulations requires an approved code of practice. No prior conviction or STR is required.

quiz.question: In the CIBC case, why did FINTRAC say an STR should have been filed for the client who had been charged?
options: The client was a foreign PEP who had not been approved
The client deposited over CAD 10,000 in cash
ML/TF indicators and known context were present, even though activity looked normal for the profile
The client had asked the bank to close the account
quiz.explanation: FINTRAC found the bank relied on the activity appearing normal while ignoring indicators and context it held, including the criminal charges.

quiz.question: Which statement about reports to FINTRAC under section 7.1 of the Act is correct?
options: Section 7.1 replaces suspicious transaction reports for any client who appears on a Canadian sanctions list
Section 7.1 applies only to money services businesses
Section 7.1 reports are sent to the RCMP instead of FINTRAC
A bank that must disclose property under sanctions or terrorism laws also reports to FINTRAC
quiz.explanation: Section 7.1 requires a report to FINTRAC when the entity must make a disclosure under section 83.1 of the Criminal Code, the UN Act, Part 1 of SEMA or the Magnitsky Law.

sessions.title: Sanctions, Ministerial directives, penalties and exam readiness
sessions.summary: Link sanctions duties to FINTRAC reporting, apply the Russia, Iran and DPRK directives, understand the 2026 penalty, compliance agreement and order regime, and prepare evidence for an examination.
objectives: Connect sanctions disclosures and sanctions evasion to FINTRAC reporting
Apply the measures required by Ministerial directives
Explain notices of violation, penalties, appeals, compliance agreements and orders
Prepare the evidence that shows an effective, risk-based program

cards.title: Stage five: the examination room
cards.setting: Boardroom, Maplecrest Bank, Toronto. Two weeks before FINTRAC arrives.

lines.text: Final stage. FINTRAC's examiners will test sanctions evasion controls, our handling of Ministerial directives and whether the program is effective.
My payments team found a wire to a trading company with a Vladivostok address. Is that a sanctions issue, a directive issue or both?
Probably both. The Russia directive applies to transactions from or to Russia regardless of amount. Sanctions laws apply if listed persons are involved.
And the board wants to know the worst case under the 2026 penalty rules. I have the numbers.
Then let's walk the examination room: sanctions, directives, penalties and the readiness checklist.

cards.title: Sanctions and directives: two systems that meet at the bank

scenes.heading: Sanctions laws prohibit dealings
scenes.narration: Canadian sanctions come mainly from the Special Economic Measures Act, the Magnitsky Law and the United Nations Act, plus the Criminal Code for listed terrorist entities. They ban dealings with listed persons.

scenes.heading: Banks keep checking
scenes.narration: Regulations under these laws require banks to determine on a continuing basis whether they hold property of listed persons, and to disclose it without delay to the authorities the law names.

scenes.heading: FINTRAC hears too
scenes.narration: When a bank must make such a disclosure, section 7.1 of the PCMLTFA requires a report to FINTRAC as well. Suspected evasion goes to FINTRAC as an STR.

scenes.heading: Directives add measures
scenes.narration: Ministerial directives do not freeze anything. They make every transaction linked to a named state high risk and add identity, due diligence and record-keeping steps.

scenes.heading: Examined and penalised
scenes.narration: FINTRAC examines compliance with directives, and breaches can lead to administrative penalties or prosecution, but not both for the same breach.

cards.title: What the Russia and DPRK directives require
cards.caption: Summarised from FINTRAC's guidance on the Russia (2024) and DPRK (2017) directives. The Iran directive (2020) is also in force; read its guidance for detail.

items.label: Treat as high risk
items.detail: Every transaction originating from or bound for the state, whatever the amount, is high risk under subsection 9.6(3).

items.label: Verify identity
items.detail: Verify anyone requesting or benefiting from the transaction, regardless of amount.

items.label: Enhanced due diligence
items.detail: Focus on sanctions evasion: source of funds, purpose and beneficial ownership or control.

items.label: Keep the record
items.detail: Keep a record of the transaction regardless of amount, as the Regulations set out.

cards.question: A client asks Maplecrest to send CAD 900 to a supplier in Russia. Which statement is correct under the Russia directive?
options: The directive does not apply below CAD 10,000
The transaction is high risk and needs identity verification, enhanced due diligence and a record regardless of amount
The bank must freeze the funds and report to the RCMP
Only an EFT report is required
cards.explanation: The directive applies to every transaction from or to Russia regardless of amount. Freezing applies only where sanctions laws are engaged.

cards.title: Sanctions law, directive or both?
cards.prompt: Sort each situation by the regime it mainly engages.

items.text: A Canadian client pays a listed person in a third country
The bank finds it holds an account of a person newly listed under SEMA
A client receives a CAD 700 family transfer from a relative in Russia
A small wire from a Canadian client to a Russian online retailer
A wire to a Russian company owned by a person listed under SEMA
An attempt to route payments to Iran through a third-country front company tied to a listed entity

cards.title: Penalties after the 2026 reforms
cards.body:
Part 4.1 of the Act, as rebuilt by the **Strengthening Canada's Immigration System and Borders Act** (S.C. 2026, c. 4, in force 26 March 2026), sets:

- **Per violation:** up to **CAD 4 million** for a person and **CAD 20 million** for an entity.
- **Per notice, all violations together:** for an entity, the greater of **CAD 20 million** and **3% of gross global revenue** in the prior financial year, using the whole affiliated group's revenue.
- **Classes:** violations remain classed as minor, serious or very serious by regulation.
- **Purpose:** penalties aim to **encourage compliance, not punish**; FINTRAC weighs the harm done and the ability to pay.
- **Compliance agreement:** after a violation is established, FINTRAC **must** require a compliance agreement with measures and a deadline.
- **Compliance order:** if the entity refuses or misses the deadline, the Director **must** issue a **public** order, and the entity must publish its remedial measures. Breaching it can cost an entity the greater of **CAD 30 million** and **3%** of gross global revenue.

cards.title: From examination to compliance order
cards.caption: Based on sections 73.14 to 73.22 of the PCMLTFA as in force since 26 March 2026.

items.label: Examination
items.detail: FINTRAC reviews records, files and systems on site or at a desk.

items.label: Notice of violation
items.detail: Names the violation and proposed penalty; 30 days to pay or make representations.

items.label: Director's decision
items.detail: On a balance of probabilities: the proposed penalty, a lesser one or none.

items.label: Appeal
items.detail: Federal Court, within 30 days, for serious, very serious or compliance order violations.

items.label: Publication
items.detail: FINTRAC publishes the name, the violation and the amount.

items.label: Compliance agreement
items.detail: Required once the violation is established, with measures and a deadline.

items.label: Compliance order
items.detail: Made public if the agreement is refused or not met in time.

lines.text: Before 2026 the per-violation caps were much lower. Now a single violation by an entity can reach CAD 20 million.
And for a group our size, 3% of global revenue is a much bigger number than CAD 20 million.
Which is why 'effective' is now in the Act. FINTRAC will ask whether our controls work, not just whether they exist.
And if we get a penalty, the compliance agreement is mandatory. If we miss it, the order is public and says what we failed to fix.

cards.title: Responding to a notice of violation
cards.situation: Months later, FINTRAC serves Maplecrest with a notice of violation proposing a penalty for missed STRs. The board chair wants to 'pay it quietly and move on'. What do you advise?

choices.text: Decide within 30 days whether to pay or make representations to the Director, plan for publication, and prepare now for the compliance agreement FINTRAC must require.
choices.outcome: Best answer. It reflects the 30-day window, the public nature of penalties and the 2026 duty to enter a compliance agreement with measures and a deadline.

choices.text: Pay quietly; payment keeps the matter confidential and ends all obligations.
choices.outcome: Paying ends the proceedings on the notice, but the violation is deemed committed, FINTRAC publishes it and a compliance agreement still follows.

choices.text: Ignore the notice until FINTRAC follows up, since nothing happens without a court order.
choices.outcome: If the bank neither pays nor makes representations within the period, it is deemed to have committed the violation and the penalty is imposed.

choices.text: Appeal straight to the Federal Court before the Director decides.
choices.outcome: The appeal right applies to the Director's decision on serious or very serious violations, or if no decision is issued within 90 days of representations. Representations come first.

cards.title: Roles in a ready bank
cards.prompt: Match each role to its main PCMLTFA responsibility at Maplecrest.

pairs.right: Implements the compliance program and keeps it current
Approves the written compliance policies and procedures
Tests program effectiveness at least every two years
Verify identity, ask questions and escalate unusual activity
Investigates referrals and files STRs as soon as practicable
Files EFT reports on time and applies directive measures

cards.back: Compliance officer, approved written policies, documented risk assessment, written ongoing training program and plan, two-year effectiveness review.
To FINTRAC, as soon as practicable once reasonable grounds to suspect are established.
Russia (2024), Iran (2020) and the DPRK (2017); FINTRAC updated its guidance on each in 2025.
CAD 20 million since 26 March 2026.
One or the other: proceeding with a violation precludes prosecuting the same act as an offence, and vice versa.
An enrolment requirement for all reporting entities was enacted in 2026 but takes effect on a date to be set by order.

cards.question: Which statement about the 2026 compliance agreement rule is correct?
options: It is optional and only offered to first-time violators
FINTRAC must require one after a violation is established
It replaces the penalty, so no money is paid
It is kept secret from the public in all cases
cards.explanation: Subsection 73.16(1) says FINTRAC shall require a compliance agreement as soon as feasible after proceedings on the violation end. Refusing or missing the deadline leads to a public compliance order.

cards.title: Real case: smaller banks are examined too (VersaBank, 2026)
cards.body:
FINTRAC's public notices show that examinations are not limited to the largest banks. On **23 February 2026**, FINTRAC imposed a penalty of **CAD 42,075** on **VersaBank**, a bank headquartered in London, Ontario, for **two violations**. The penalty was paid in full and the case closed.

In **2025**, First Nations Bank of Canada received a penalty of about **CAD 601,000** for five violations, and in **2024** Exchange Bank of Canada received one of about **CAD 2.46 million**, later varied by the Federal Court.

The lesson for a mid-sized bank like Maplecrest: size does not protect you, and a public notice names the bank whatever the amount.

cards.title: Real case: one root cause, five violations (TD, 2024)
Stage five take-aways
items: Sanctions laws ban dealings and require continuing checks and disclosure; section 7.1 adds a report to FINTRAC.
Suspected sanctions evasion is reported to FINTRAC through an STR.
Directives on Russia, Iran and the DPRK make linked transactions high risk regardless of amount.
Since 26 March 2026: up to CAD 20 million per violation for an entity, a cap per notice of the greater of CAD 20 million and 3% of group revenue.
A compliance agreement is mandatory after a violation; missing it brings a public compliance order.
Readiness means evidence: approved policies, current risk assessment, training records, review reports and filed reports.

cards.prompt: If FINTRAC examined your team next month, which piece of evidence would be hardest to produce: training records, risk assessment updates, investigation notes or report timeliness? What would you fix first?

quiz.question: Which laws are the main sources of Canadian sanctions referred to in the PCMLTFA definition of a sanctions evasion offence?
options: The Bank Act, the Criminal Code and PIPEDA
The Customs Act, the Excise Act and the Income Tax Act
The United Nations Act, Part 1 of SEMA and the Sergei Magnitsky Law
The Competition Act, the Investment Canada Act and SEMA Part 2
