quiz.explanation: The Act defines a sanctions evasion offence as breaching a restriction under the UN Act, Part 1 of SEMA or the Magnitsky Law.

quiz.question: Maplecrest discovers that an account belongs to a person newly listed under a SEMA regulation and makes the disclosure the sanctions regulation requires. What else does the PCMLTFA require?
options: Nothing further, because sanctions are outside the PCMLTFA
A report to FINTRAC under section 7.1
A large cash report for the account balance
A notice to the client explaining the freeze and the report
quiz.explanation: Section 7.1 requires reporting entities that must disclose under the Criminal Code, UN Act regulations, SEMA Part 1 regulations or the Magnitsky Law to report to FINTRAC as well.

quiz.question: A client sends CAD 400 to a relative in North Korea. What does the DPRK directive require?
options: Nothing, because the amount is below the CAD 1,000 identity verification threshold for international transfers
Block it and report it to the RCMP within 24 hours
File an EFT report only
Treat as high risk, verify identity, apply sanctions-focused due diligence, keep a record
quiz.explanation: FINTRAC's guidance on the DPRK directive applies its measures to every transaction from or to North Korea regardless of amount.

quiz.question: How often must Ministerial directives be reviewed, according to FINTRAC's directives page?
options: At least every three years from the day they take effect
Every year at the federal budget
Only when the FATF changes its lists
Every five years by Parliament
quiz.explanation: FINTRAC states that directives remain in force until revoked, suspended or amended and are reviewed at least every three years.

quiz.question: Since 26 March 2026, what is the maximum penalty for a single prescribed violation committed by an entity?
options: CAD 20 million
CAD 4 million
CAD 30 million
quiz.explanation: Subsection 73.1(2) sets CAD 20 million per violation for an entity and CAD 4 million for a person. CAD 30 million is the floor of the compliance order violation cap.

quiz.question: For an entity in an affiliated group, how is the 3% cumulative cap per notice of violation calculated?
options: On the whole affiliated group's gross global revenue for the prior year
On the Canadian revenue of the branch or business line that actually committed the violation
On the bank's net profit in the year of the violation
On the total value of the unreported transactions
quiz.explanation: Subsection 73.1(4) deems the entity's gross global revenue to be that of the affiliated group for the prior financial year.

quiz.question: What must the Director do if an entity refuses to enter into a compliance agreement?
options: Cancel the original penalty
Make a compliance order and make it public
Refer the entity directly for criminal prosecution
Extend the deadline by two years automatically
quiz.explanation: Section 73.17 requires a compliance order, which must be made public and require the entity to publish its measures.

quiz.question: Which criteria must FINTRAC consider when setting a penalty under section 73.11?
options: The bank's share price and credit rating
Encouraging compliance, the harm done, and the ability to pay
Only the number of transactions affected and the total dollar value involved in them
The salary of the compliance officer
quiz.explanation: Section 73.11 lists the compliance-not-punishment purpose, the harm done, the ability to pay and any prescribed criteria.

quiz.question: A bank makes representations on a notice of violation. What standard does the Director apply?
options: Beyond reasonable doubt
Reasonable grounds to suspect
Clear and convincing evidence
Balance of probabilities
quiz.explanation: Subsection 73.15(2) requires the Director to decide on a balance of probabilities and allows the proposed penalty, a lesser one or none.

quiz.question: What is the status of the 2026 enrolment requirement for all reporting entities?
options: Enacted in 2026 but coming into force on a date to be fixed by order
In force since 26 March 2026 for every bank
Applies only to money services businesses already registered
Withdrawn before royal assent
quiz.explanation: The Strengthening Canada's Immigration System and Borders Act added enrolment provisions, but they come into force on a day fixed by order of the Governor in Council.

regulators: Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC)
Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada (codes of practice under section 11.01)

references.title: Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Regulations (SOR/2002-184)
references.provision: Section 156(1)(d) and (e) (training program and plan); 156(3) (two-year review)
references.note: The compliance program must include a written, ongoing compliance training program for employees, agents and others authorised to act for the entity, a documented plan for delivering that training, and a documented effectiveness review at least every two years.

references.title: Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (S.C. 2000, c. 17)
references.provision: Section 9.6(1) and (1.1) (compliance program); 9.6(3) (special measures for high risk)
references.note: Every reporting entity must establish and implement a compliance program in line with the Regulations; since March 2026 the program must also be reasonably designed, risk-based and effective.

references.title: Compliance program requirements
references.note: FINTRAC expects the training program to explain the Act's requirements, the entity's policies on reporting, record keeping and know-your-client, and each person's role in detecting ML/TF; the plan should name recipients, topics, methods and frequency, tailored to ML, TF and sanctions evasion risk.

references.title: Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (S.C. 2000, c. 17)
references.provision: Sections 7 (suspicious transactions), 7.1 (property disclosures), 8 (no disclosure), 9.2 (anonymous accounts) and 9.3 (PEPs)
references.note: Report completed or attempted transactions where there are reasonable grounds to suspect ML, TF or sanctions evasion; report to FINTRAC when a sanctions or terrorist property disclosure is required; do not disclose reports to prejudice an investigation.

references.title: Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (S.C. 2000, c. 17)
references.provision: Part 4.1, sections 73.1-73.22 (penalties, compliance agreements and orders, appeals, publication)
references.note: Since March 2026: up to $4 million per violation for a person and $20 million for an entity; per-notice cap of the greater of $20 million and 3% of group gross global revenue; mandatory compliance agreements and public compliance orders.

references.title: Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (S.C. 2000, c. 17)
references.provision: Section 11.01 (disclosure, collection and use of personal information)
references.note: Reporting entities may share personal information with each other without consent to detect or deter ML, TF or sanctions evasion when the statutory conditions are met; good-faith sharing is protected.

references.title: Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Regulations (SOR/2002-184)
references.note: Report cash and international EFTs of $10,000 or more (aggregated over 24 hours), cash within 15 days and EFTs within 5 working days; keep records at least five years and produce them within 30 days.

references.title: Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Regulations (SOR/2002-184)
references.note: Identity verification triggers and methods, PEP and HIO rules (five-year period for domestic PEPs and HIOs), third-party determination, beneficial ownership and discrepancy reports, special measures, and codes of practice for information sharing.

references.title: Ministerial directives and transaction restrictions
references.note: Lists Ministerial directives under Part 1.1 of the Act for Russia (2024), Iran (2020) and the DPRK (2017); linked guidance requires treating covered transactions as high risk regardless of amount.

references.title: Reporting suspicious transactions to FINTRAC
references.note: Explains reasonable grounds to suspect, the as-soon-as-practicable deadline, the absence of a monetary threshold and how to avoid tipping off.

references.title: Public notice of administrative monetary penalties
references.note: Lists penalties imposed, including on The Toronto-Dominion Bank (2024), Royal Bank of Canada (2023), CIBC (2023), Exchange Bank of Canada (2024) and First Nations Bank of Canada (2025).

references.title: Strengthening Canada's Immigration System and Borders Act (S.C. 2026, c. 4)
references.provision: Part 9 (amendments to the PCMLTFA); section 124 (coming into force)
references.note: Added the effective-program requirement, rebuilt the penalty regime and enacted an enrolment requirement whose provisions come into force on a day fixed by order.

bank.question: A new analyst says Maplecrest's AML duties come mainly from OSFI guidelines. Which correction is most accurate?
options: The duties come from the PCMLTFA and its Regulations, supervised by FINTRAC
The duties come from the Bank Act and are supervised by FCAC
The duties come from FATF Recommendations, which apply directly in Canada
The duties come from provincial securities law and each province's regulator
bank.explanation: Canadian banks' AML/ATF duties are set by the PCMLTFA and Regulations and supervised by FINTRAC. FATF standards shape the law but do not apply directly.

bank.question: Under the Regulations, who is responsible for complying with the Regulations when a teller performs a covered transaction for the bank?
options: The teller personally, with the bank as guarantor
The branch manager personally for each branch
The bank as employer, rather than the individual teller
FINTRAC, which supervises the transaction in real time
bank.explanation: Subsection 133(1) makes the employer, not the employee, responsible for complying with the Regulations. Staff still follow the bank's procedures.

bank.question: Which description of a 'terrorist activity financing offence' matches the PCMLTFA definition?
options: Any transaction at all with a person from a country that is currently covered by a Ministerial directive
Any cash deposit over CAD 10,000 by a non-resident
Any breach of the Special Economic Measures Act
Criminal Code terrorist financing offences, including dealing in terrorist property
bank.explanation: The Act defines it by reference to sections 83.02 to 83.04 of the Criminal Code and section 83.12 arising from section 83.08 (dealing in terrorist property). SEMA breaches are sanctions evasion offences.

bank.question: Kwame's team sees payments that seem designed to help a person listed under the Magnitsky Law move money out of Canada. Which PCMLTFA duty is most directly engaged?
options: A large cash transaction report under the Regulations
An STR for a suspected sanctions evasion offence under section 7(c)
A beneficial ownership discrepancy report to Corporations Canada
An effectiveness review by internal audit within 30 days
bank.explanation: Breaching a prohibition under the Magnitsky Law is a sanctions evasion offence, so reasonable grounds to suspect trigger an STR under section 7(c).

bank.question: Which change did the 2026 amendments make to subsection 9.6 of the PCMLTFA?
options: It removed the need for a documented risk assessment for banks with a strong examination history
Required all STRs to be approved by the board
A duty to make the program reasonably designed, risk-based and effective
Moved AML supervision from FINTRAC to OSFI
bank.explanation: New subsection 9.6(1.1), in force 26 March 2026, adds the reasonably designed, risk-based and effective standard. FINTRAC remains the supervisor.

bank.question: Which of these is the official name of the 2026 statute that rebuilt FINTRAC's penalty regime?
options: Strengthening Canada's Immigration System and Borders Act (S.C. 2026, c. 4)
Financial Crime Accountability Act (S.C. 2026, c. 1)
Proceeds of Crime Modernization Act (S.C. 2026, c. 7)
Anti-Money Laundering Enforcement Act (S.C. 2026, c. 2)
bank.explanation: Part 9 of S.C. 2026, c. 4, the Strengthening Canada's Immigration System and Borders Act, amended the PCMLTFA's penalty, compliance order and program provisions. The other titles are invented.

bank.question: A board member asks whether FINTRAC can both prosecute and impose an administrative penalty for the same failure. What is correct?
options: No; proceeding as a violation precludes proceeding as an offence
Yes; both always run in parallel
Yes, but only for very serious violations
No; FINTRAC can only prosecute through the courts and can never impose administrative penalties
bank.explanation: Section 73.12 says that proceeding in one manner precludes the other. FINTRAC's directives page makes the same point.

bank.question: In the RBC case, FINTRAC found STRs that combined transactions from several branch locations. Why did that matter?
options: It made each report too short to be useful
It meant the reports were filed before the end of the 24-hour aggregation window had passed
It exposed client names to other branches
Reports must be separate by location, so the location data was wrong
bank.explanation: FINTRAC found 29 of 34 sampled STRs mixed locations, so the location in the report was incorrect, contrary to its published reporting instructions.

bank.question: What does FINTRAC say about the length of time notices of administrative monetary penalties stay on its website?
options: They are removed once the penalty is paid
They remain on the public website for five years
They stay for one year after the appeal period
They are never published unless the entity agrees
bank.explanation: FINTRAC's public notice page states that notices remain on its website for five years.

bank.question: Which list correctly states the compliance program elements in subsection 156(1) of the Regulations?
options: Board charter, annual STR quota, client exit policy, quarterly audit, FINTRAC certificate, OSFI rating and a sanctions screening tool approval
Risk appetite, capital plan, liquidity plan, recovery plan, resolution plan
Responsible person, approved written policies, documented risk assessment, written ongoing training program and plan, effectiveness review plan
Compliance officer, sanctions list, privacy notice, complaints process, whistleblowing line
bank.explanation: Paragraphs 156(1)(a) to (f) set these elements. FINTRAC groups the training program and its plan together as one element.

bank.question: Maplecrest's training plan says only branch staff receive AML training. Based on FINTRAC's guidance, which gap would an examiner most likely raise?
options: Recipients such as the compliance officer, senior management, IT and audit are missing
Branch staff should not receive AML training at all
Training should be given only by FINTRAC staff or by a trainer that FINTRAC has formally accredited for the bank
Training records should not show attendees' names
bank.explanation: FINTRAC's guidance lists recipients beyond front-line staff, including the compliance officer, senior management, IT and internal audit, depending on duties.

bank.question: Which statement about training frequency matches FINTRAC's guidance?
options: It must be exactly once every calendar year for every employee, with the same content for all roles
The bank sets it in its plan: regular intervals, event triggers or both
It is required only when FINTRAC issues new guidance
It must be monthly for front-line staff and never for managers
bank.explanation: FINTRAC says training can be at regular intervals, on events such as a new hire or procedure change, or both, tailored to the entity's size, complexity and risk.

bank.question: Mei's new teller will serve clients from her second day. What does FINTRAC's guidance suggest about timing her AML training?
options: She can wait until the next annual training session, whenever that falls in the bank's calendar year
She must first pass a FINTRAC-run certification exam
FINTRAC gives 'before a new employee deals with clients' as an example
Training is not needed if she shadows an experienced teller
bank.explanation: FINTRAC gives 'before a new employee deals with clients' as an example of event-driven training timing.

bank.question: What should a bank keep to show that its ongoing training program is actually delivered?
options: Copies of each employee's performance appraisal
A list of clients each employee onboarded
Only the vendor's invoice for the training
Records of delivery, such as dates, attendees and topics covered
bank.explanation: FINTRAC's guidance says the training program should include a record of training delivered, such as dates, attendees and topics.

bank.question: Kwame wants to add a new correspondent relationship in a high-risk region. Which risk assessment factor in paragraph 156(1)(c) most directly covers this?
options: The effectiveness review plan
Clients, business relationships and correspondent banking relationships
The training methods for delivery
The approval of policies by a senior officer
bank.explanation: Subparagraph 156(1)(c)(i) explicitly names correspondent banking relationships among the risk factors; geography under (iii) would also apply.

bank.question: A bank with no internal or external auditor must run its two-year effectiveness review. Who carries it out?
options: FINTRAC's examiners
The entity itself
OSFI's supervisory team
A peer bank chosen by FINTRAC
bank.explanation: Subsection 156(3) allows the entity itself to do the review only if it has no auditor. Banks normally use internal audit.

bank.question: Which three items must the written report to a senior officer contain after the effectiveness review?
options: The names of all STR subjects, their balances and their addresses
The training scores of each employee, their grades and their managers
The review findings, policy updates in the period, and the status of implementing them
The board minutes, the budget and the bank's credit rating
bank.explanation: Subsection 156(4) requires findings, updates made to policies and procedures in the reporting period, and the status of their implementation.

bank.question: In the First Nations Bank of Canada case, how did FINTRAC classify the failure to report suspicious transactions?
options: As a minor violation
As a serious violation
As a very serious violation
As a compliance order violation
bank.explanation: FINTRAC's notice classified the STR failure as very serious; the policy, risk assessment and special measures failures as serious; and ongoing monitoring as minor.

bank.question: A client cannot be identified using any method in the Regulations, but insists on opening a savings account. What does the Act say?
options: Open the account but block withdrawals for 90 days
Open the account and file an STR the same day
Open the account if a branch manager signs off
The bank must not open an anonymous account or one for an anonymous client
bank.explanation: Section 9.2 prohibits opening an anonymous account or an account for a client whose identity cannot be verified as the Regulations require.

bank.question: Under the dual-process method, which combination would be acceptable?
options: One photo of the client plus the client's own signed written statement of their current home address
Two documents from the same source, both showing name and address
One source confirming name and address, another confirming name and date of birth
A social media profile plus the client's business card
bank.explanation: Paragraph 105(1)(d) requires two of the listed confirmations, and subsection 105(4) says the information must not come from the same source, nor from the client or the bank itself.

bank.question: A walk-in client asks to exchange CAD 3,200 into euros. What does section 86 require?
options: Verify identity: foreign exchange of CAD 3,000 or more triggers it
Nothing, because only account openings require verification
Verify identity only above CAD 10,000
File a large cash transaction report, regardless of how the client pays for the currency exchange
bank.explanation: Section 86 requires verification for foreign currency exchanges of CAD 3,000 or more by non-account clients.

bank.question: Maplecrest is onboarding a family trust. Which information must it obtain under section 138?
options: Only the name of the lawyer who drafted the trust deed
Only beneficiaries who own 25% or more of the trust assets
Only the name of the trust and its tax number
Names and addresses of all trustees and all known beneficiaries and settlors
bank.explanation: Paragraph 138(1)(b) requires names and addresses of all trustees and all known beneficiaries and settlors, plus ownership, control and structure.

bank.question: Which discrepancy would NOT be treated as material under section 138.1?
options: A different person shown as a 25% owner in the registry
A minor spelling variation in a beneficial owner's name
A director missing from the client's declaration
An extra controlling shareholder listed in the registry
bank.explanation: Subsection 138.1(3) excludes spelling errors and minor name or address variations from material discrepancies.

bank.question: A new account holder is the brother of a serving foreign head of state. What follows under the Regulations?
options: He is outside the PEP rules entirely because he holds no public office himself in any country
He is a domestic PEP because he lives in Canada
Only an EFT report is required for his transfers
He is a foreign PEP's family member, so the foreign PEP measures apply
bank.explanation: Section 121(1) applies the foreign PEP measures to prescribed family members and close associates of a politically exposed foreign person.

bank.question: Maplecrest finally receives an international EFT of CAD 150,000 for a beneficiary it determines is a foreign PEP. What must happen?
options: A member of senior management must review the transaction
The funds must be returned to the sender
The beneficiary's account must be closed within 30 days
Nothing beyond the EFT report
bank.explanation: Subsection 122(3) requires senior management review where the beneficiary of a CAD 100,000-plus international EFT is a foreign PEP, family member or close associate.

bank.question: When opening a business account, the signer says employees of a related company will also use it. Which duty is engaged?
options: Large cash transaction reporting, because business accounts of this kind usually handle large amounts of cash
A section 11.01 disclosure to the related company's bank
Third-party determination, with reasonable measures and records
A Ministerial directive review
bank.explanation: Section 135 requires reasonable measures at account opening to determine whether the account will be used by or on behalf of a third party, and records of the information.

bank.question: Which purpose is NOT part of ongoing monitoring under section 123.1?
options: Detecting transactions that must be reported
Keeping beneficial ownership information up to date
Reassessing the risk level of the client's activity
Setting the client's interest rate for the next term
bank.explanation: Section 123.1 covers detecting reportable transactions, updating information, reassessing risk and checking consistency. Pricing is a business decision.

bank.question: Harpreet's team closed an alert because 'there is no proof the funds came from crime'. What is wrong with that reasoning?
options: Proof is required, but only for terrorist financing cases
Alerts can be closed only by FINTRAC
The test is reasonable grounds to believe, which was clearly not met on the facts in this file
The test is reasonable grounds to suspect; proof is not needed
bank.explanation: FINTRAC's guidance says you do not need to verify facts or prove an offence to reach reasonable grounds to suspect.

bank.question: A production order arrives for a client, and the client's activity shows several ML indicators. Based on the RBC and TD cases, what should the bank's procedure ensure?
options: The order is filed with legal and no further review is needed
The client is told about the order so they can respond
The file is escalated so the FIU can decide whether an STR is required
The account is closed and the STR question is dropped
bank.explanation: Both notices criticised failures to escalate or review production order files for STR decisions. Telling the client risks tipping off.

bank.question: Which information must NOT be requested from a client purely because you are preparing an STR, according to FINTRAC's guidance?
options: Information you would not normally ask for, if asking could tip the client off
Information that you normally collect for that type of transaction
Identity details required by the Regulations
Information already held within the bank's own systems
bank.explanation: FINTRAC warns against requesting information you would not normally request if it might tip off the client, and expects you to report what you already hold.

bank.question: A client deposits CAD 9,000 cash in the morning and CAD 1,500 cash in the afternoon to an account for the same beneficiary, and the bank knows this. Which report is due, and by when?
options: An EFT report, within 5 working days
No report, because each deposit is below CAD 10,000
An STR, within 24 hours
A large cash transaction report, within 15 days
bank.explanation: The 24-hour rule in section 126 aggregates the deposits into one CAD 10,500 cash transaction, and subsection 132(3) gives 15 days. An STR is separate and depends on suspicion.

bank.question: CIBC's 2023 penalty included unreported incoming EFTs. What role did FINTRAC say the bank played in those transfers?
options: It was the last Canadian financial institution to receive the international EFTs
It was the ordering institution sending funds abroad
It was an intermediary that never handled client funds
It was the correspondent of a foreign shell bank
bank.explanation: FINTRAC found 1,003 instances where CIBC was the last Canadian financial institution to receive the international EFT and should have reported it.

bank.question: An entity record proving a corporation's existence was collected when the client relationship began. How long must it be kept?
options: At least five years after the day of the last business transaction
At least five years after the day it was created
At least five years after the account opened
Until the corporation is dissolved
bank.explanation: Paragraph 148(1)(b) measures the five years from the last business transaction for records that prove an entity's existence.

bank.question: FINTRAC asks to examine records held in an archive. How quickly must they be provided?
options: Within 24 hours
Within 30 days after the request
Within 5 working days
Within 90 days
bank.explanation: Section 149 requires records to be kept so they can be provided within 30 days of a request under section 62 of the Act.

bank.question: Which condition is part of section 11.01 for disclosing personal information to another reporting entity without consent?
options: Seeking consent would risk compromising detection or deterrence
The person has already been convicted of a money laundering or terrorist financing offence in Canada
FINTRAC has asked both entities to share the information
The information was bought from a third-party data broker
bank.explanation: Section 11.01 requires, among other things, that disclosure with knowledge or consent would risk compromising the ability to detect or deter ML, TF or sanctions evasion.

bank.question: Who approves the code of practice that a reporting entity needs before using section 11.01?
options: The Privacy Commissioner of Canada
The Director of FINTRAC
The Superintendent of Financial Institutions
The Minister of Finance
bank.explanation: Section 159 and following in the Regulations require a code of practice approved by the Privacy Commissioner; FINTRAC is notified and may comment.

bank.question: Under the Russia directive, which factor does FINTRAC say can indicate that a transaction is bound for or from Russia?
options: Any transaction by a client with a Slavic-sounding name
Any payment made by card while the client travels in Europe
A transfer with a Russian originating or destination address, or ruble deposits or exchanges
Any transfer in US dollars
bank.explanation: FINTRAC's guidance points to facts such as Russian addresses, Russian government representatives and ruble deposits or exchanges. Names alone are not an indicator.

bank.question: What does the Russia directive require the bank to focus on when it exercises customer due diligence for a covered transaction?
options: The client's credit history, repayment capacity and the bank's internal credit score for the client
Sanctions evasion risk: source of funds, purpose and ownership or control
The client's tax residency for CRS reporting
The client's marketing preferences and consent
bank.explanation: The directive requires due diligence with particular attention to sanctions evasion, including source of funds, purpose and the beneficial ownership or control of entities.

bank.question: Maplecrest pays a penalty proposed in a notice of violation. What is the legal effect?
options: It is deemed to have committed the violation and proceedings on that notice end
The violation is withdrawn and nothing is published
The penalty is held in trust until an appeal is decided
The bank is exempt from examination for two years
bank.explanation: Subsection 73.15(1) deems the violation committed and ends proceedings. FINTRAC then publishes it and requires a compliance agreement.

bank.question: A bank neither pays nor makes representations within the period in the notice of violation. What happens?
options: The notice lapses and FINTRAC must start again
The case goes automatically to the Federal Court
The penalty is halved for late response
It is deemed to have committed the violation and FINTRAC imposes the proposed penalty
bank.explanation: Subsection 73.15(3) deems the violation committed and requires FINTRAC to impose the proposed penalty.

bank.question: Within what period may an entity appeal the Director's decision on a serious violation to the Federal Court?
options: Within 5 working days after the examination ends, before any notice of violation is issued at all
Within 90 days after the penalty is paid
Within one year after publication
Within 30 days after service of the decision, or longer if the Court allows
bank.explanation: Subsection 73.21(1) sets 30 days after service, or any longer period the Court allows, for serious, very serious and compliance order violations.

bank.question: What maximum penalty applies to a compliance order violation by an entity?
options: A flat CAD 20 million with no revenue-based alternative
The greater of CAD 30 million and 3% of gross global revenue
The greater of CAD 4 million and 1% of the bank's Canadian revenue in the year of the breach
Twice the penalty in the original notice of violation
bank.explanation: Subsection 73.18(2) caps a compliance order violation by an entity at the greater of CAD 30 million and 3% of gross global revenue, using group revenue for affiliates.

bank.question: What must a compliance order require of the entity, besides complying with the provision by a deadline?
options: That it replace its entire board within 90 days
That it make public the measures taken or to be taken to comply
That it stop accepting new clients until FINTRAC re-examines it
That it pay the costs of FINTRAC's examination
bank.explanation: Subsection 73.17(2) requires the order to include compliance with the provision, public disclosure of the measures, and a deadline.

bank.question: The TD case showed one root cause producing several violations. What was that root cause, according to FINTRAC?
options: A cyber attack that deleted transaction records
Weak oversight of client risk rating, so high-risk clients were not identified
A shortage of tellers in branches
A failure to register with FINTRAC
bank.explanation: FINTRAC traced the risk assessment, special measures, ongoing monitoring and record-keeping failures to weak oversight of client risk rating solutions during a transition.

bank.question: Elise prepares the examination evidence pack. Which set of documents best shows an effective, risk-based program in FINTRAC's eyes?
options: The bank's annual report, its marketing plan, its share register and its latest investor presentation slides
A FINTRAC certificate, an OSFI rating and a privacy notice
Approved policies, risk assessment, training records, review report, timely reports
Branch opening hours, product brochures and fee schedules
bank.explanation: Examiners test each program element and whether it works, so evidence of each element plus timely reporting is what demonstrates effectiveness.
